summary: This Lunar Navigator (or as I like to call it, the Henry-gator!) ranks possible Artemis landing spots at the Moon's south pole by exact coordinates and landing date. A polar lander needs ample Sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communications at the same time, but both are scarce there: the Sun skims the horizon, craters and ridges block it, and Earth drifts in and out of view. Henry-gator answers "where, and when?" using real NASA data. It simulates the Sun and Earth over the Moon's full 18.6-year cycle behind the true terrain skyline at any point, tries every possible landing date for a 6.5-day stay, and reports the best landing-date ranges. Users set hard requirements, such as maximum slope and minimum sunlight, and adjust the weights that rank the surviving sites. Every result is checked against NASA's own published sunlight and Earth-visibility maps: across 60 random points near the pole, our simulation matches NASA's sunlight map at 0.99 correlation with a typical error of 1.8 percentage points, and 93% of points agree within 3 points. The tool also compares sites that researchers proposed inside NASA's 13 Artemis III candidate regions.
details:
What it does and how it works?
Henry-gator helps answer where and when a crewed lander could touch down at the Moon's south pole. At the pole the Sun barely clears the horizon and terrain blocks it, while Earth sits low in the sky, so power and communications are scarce and shifting. The tool computes the Sun's and Earth's positions from NASA/JPL ephemeris data, treats both as real discs seen from the surface, and compares their paths with the terrain skyline built from NASA's LOLA elevation data. It does this over the Moon's full 18.6 year cycle. For a mission stay (6.5 days by default as planned for Artemis III) it tries every possible landing date and reports the best landing-date ranges. It also finds candidate spots automatically from NASA's maps, ranks them by exact latitude and longitude, and applies pass/fail requirements (slope, sunlight, Earth link) plus user-set weights to accommodate for specific mission preferences. Each candidate is refined to a single 60 m map pixel, so every result is a specific latitude and longitude, accurate to about 10 m.

Benefits and intended impact?
Mission planners and students can compare sites and dates quickly and see why one beats another, instead of reading raw map layers. The intended impact is to make polar landing-site reasoning transparent, checkable and open to anyone. A built-in accuracy check compares the simulation with NASA's published maps: across 60 random points near the pole it matches NASA's sunlight map at 0.99 correlation (typical error 1.8 points) and Earth visibility at 0.99 (2.5 points).

Tools?
Python 3.11 (FastAPI, Skyfield, Rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, httpx), JavaScript with Leaflet and Plotly.js, HTML and CSS. NASA data: LOLA elevation, NASA illumination and Earth-visibility maps, Moon Trek imagery, ShadowCam mosaics, JPL DE421 ephemeris. No special hardware: it runs on a laptop. Source is on GitHub. I used an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) for research and Troubleshooting and I directed the direction, design, data choices, logic and validation. Everything runs on real NASA and JPL data with no mock-ups, and I audited every downloaded file against NASA's servers for completeness, map projection and plausible values.

Creativity!
Four weight sliders can adjust the landing site ranking based on what a specific mission aims to achieve. The accuracy check is built into the interface, so users can test my claims against NASA's own data. The zoomable polar map switches between NASA imagery, elevation and shaded relief (computed with adjustable lighting), and overlays sunlight, Earth visibility and ShadowCam photos of permanently dark craters. The 2.7 GB high-resolution terrain is fetched tile by tile, only where needed. Landing results are shown as date ranges with slack, not single dates. Earth link accounts for NASA's Deep Space Network stations, not just Earth being above the horizon.

Factors considered :)
Physical realism was important (curved Moon, terrain horizons that dip below flat ground, finite Sun and Earth discs, parallax). When my results first differed from NASA's, I tested competing explanations one at a time (Earth's size, parallax, compass-direction resolution, time span, terrain resolution) and changed the model only where the evidence supported it. Honest validation: I found and fixed one of my own errors, and noted that two published site claims are not fully supported by NASA's maps. NASA does not state the observer height behind its maps, so I calibrated that for the comparison only. I state the limits plainly: sites are screening candidates, not official NASA sites, and there is no battery or thermal model.
